'''Reatha Belle Clark King''' (born April 11, 1938) is an American [[chemist]], the former vice president of the [[General Mills, Inc.|General Mills Corporation]]; and the former president, executive director, and chairman of the board of trustees of the General Mills Foundation, the philanthropic foundation of [[General Mills, Inc.]]

==Early life and education==
Reatha Belle Clark<ref name="Yount">{{cite book |last1=Yount |first1=Lisa |title=A to Z of women in science and math |date=2008 |publisher=Facts On File, Inc.|location=New York |isbn=978-0816066957 |pages=156–157 |edition=Rev. |url=https://www.mobt3ath.com/uplode/book/book-24728.pdf |access-date=24 October 2018}}</ref> was born in [[Pavo, Georgia]], United States on April 11, 1938.<ref name ="Brown2012">{{cite book|last=Brown|first=Jeannette E.|title=African American women chemists|url=https://archive.org/details/africanamericanw00brow|url-access=limited|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|date=2012| isbn=9780199742882 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/africanamericanw00brow/page/n127 115]–123}}</ref><ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title=  Reatha Clark King |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/king-reatha-clark|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref> Her father, Willie B. Clark, was a [[sharecropper]], and her mother, Ola Mae Watts Campbell, had only a third-grade education.<ref name="transcript">{{cite book|first=Jeannette E. |last=Brown|title= Reatha Clark King, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by Jeannette E. Brown at Minneapolis, Minnesota on 1 May 2005 |date=1 May 2005 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/king_rc_0663_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Science History Institute|Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref><ref name="Jenkins">{{cite book |last1=Jenkins |first1=Edward Sidney |title=To fathom more : African American scientists and inventors |date=1996 |publisher=University Press of America |location=Lanham, Md. |isbn=978-0761802150 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/tofathommoreafri0000jenk/page/342 342–368] |chapter=Reatha Clark King: Chemistry of the Halogen Compounds (1938- ) |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/tofathommoreafri0000jenk/ |url=https://archive.org/details/tofathommoreafri0000jenk/page/342 }}</ref>

Reatha Clark began elementary school in a one-room school for grades 1&ndash;7, at Mt. Zion Baptist, a colored church, where she was taught by Florence Frazier.<ref name="Equality"/>  Later, she attended school in Coolidge, Georgia, and high school in Moultrie, Georgia.<ref name="transcript"/> When she graduated from Moultrie High School for Negro Youth in 1954, the same year that ''[[Brown v. Board of Education]]'' determined segregated schools were illegal,  Clark was the valedictorian of her class.<ref name="Tuttle"/><ref name="Equality">{{cite web|title=Equality through education and giving, Reatha Clark|url=http://www.aaregistry.org/historic_events/view/equality-through-education-and-giving-reatha-clark-king|publisher=African American Registry|access-date=13 May 2014}}</ref>

Clark was recruited to attend [[Clark Atlanta University|Clark College in Atlanta]], where she initially enrolled as a home economics major.  She was encouraged to become a research chemist by the head of the chemistry department there, Alfred Spriggs.<ref name="transcript"/> King earned a bachelor of science degree in chemistry and mathematics from Clark College.<ref name="transcript"/>

Spriggs encouraged her to apply for a fellowship from the [[Woodrow Wilson National Fellowship Foundation]], which she received from 1958 to 1960.<ref name ="Brown2012"/> The fellowship supported her work at the [[University of Chicago]], from which she obtained a master of science degree in chemistry in 1960. She went on to study with advisor [[Ole J. Kleppa]], receiving her Ph.D. degree in [[thermochemistry]] from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1963.  The title of her Ph.D. thesis was "Contributions to the thermochemistry of the [[Laves phases]]."<ref name="Makers">{{cite web|title=Reatha Clark King|url=http://www.thehistorymakers.com/biography/reatha-clark-king-42|publisher=The HistoryMakers|access-date=13 May 2014|date=2012-01-16}}</ref> 
While in Chicago she also met and married N. Judge King.<ref name="Tuttle">{{cite journal|last=Tuttle|first=Kelly|title=For the Love of the Lab|journal=Chemical Heritage Magazine|date=2012 |volume=30|issue=2|page=38|access-date=6 December 2016|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/distillations/magazine/for-love-of-the-lab}}</ref>

Reatha Clark King later earned a master's in business administration in [[finance]] management from [[Columbia University]] while on sabbatical.<ref name="Grotto">{{cite web|title=Reatha Clark King—2004-05 Louis W. Hill, Jr. Fellow|url=http://www.grottofoundation.org/fellowship/king|publisher=Grotto Foundation|access-date=13 May 2014|url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141216010733/https://grottofoundation.org/fellowship/king |archive-date=December 16, 2014 }}</ref>

==Scientific and academic career==
King was employed for five years (1963–1968) as a research chemist for the [[National Bureau of Standards]] in Washington, D.C. Hired by [[George T. Armstrong]], King was the first African American female chemist to work at the agency.<ref name ="Brown2012"/><ref name="Makers"/> She used techniques for both bomb and flame calorimetry.<ref name="Domalski">{{cite journal |last1=Domalski |first1=Eugene S. |title=Evaluating Experimental Data on Heats of Combustion |journal=Journal of Chemical Documentation |date=November 1971 |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=234–238 |doi=10.1021/c160043a014|quote=Basically, two main experimental techniques are employed to obtain the heats of combustion, bomb calorimetry (combustion process at constant volume), and flame or flow calorimetry (combustion process at constant pressure). Flame calorimetry is more applicable to the combustion of gaseous or highly volatile substances, whereas bomb calorimetry is more suited to studying liquids and solids.}}</ref> Much of her work there involved measuring the accurate heats of formation of gaseous [[fluorine]] compounds,<ref name="Grotto"/> and she received a Meritorious Publication Award for her paper on fluoride flame calorimetry.<ref name="Makers"/> This research was important to the [[NASA]] space program.<ref name="Grotto"/>  Her two children were born during this time.<ref name="transcript"/> Techniques and mechanisms that she developed for flame fluorine calorimetry are still used.<ref name="Simões">{{cite book |last1=Simões |first1=José A. Martinho |last2=Piedade |first2=Manuel Minas da |title=Molecular Energetics : Condensed-Phase Thermochemical Techniques. |date=July 10, 2008 |publisher=Oxford University Press, USA |isbn=9780195133196 |pages=120– |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vXc8DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA120 |quote=Jessup and Armstrong and their colleagues [109, 115-117] developed the method of fluorine flame calorimetry to a high degree of accuracy and precision. |access-date=18 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="Lykknes">{{cite book |last1=Mark Ockerbloom |first1=Mary  |chapter= Reatha Clark King, Starting Fires with Fluorine |editor-last1=Lykknes |editor-first1=Annette |editor-last2=Van Tiggelen |editor-first2=Brigitte|editor2-link=Brigitte Van Tiggelen |title=Women in Their Element: Selected Women's Contributions To The Periodic System |date=2019 |publisher=World Scientific |location=Singapore }}</ref>

King and her family moved to New York when her husband accepted a position at [[Nassau Community College]], [[Garden City, New York]]. King obtained an assistant professorship at [[York College, City University of New York]].  There she served as professor of chemistry, 1968–1977, associate dean for Division of Natural Science & Mathematics, 1970-1974, and associate dean for academic affairs, 1974–1977.<ref name="transcript"/>

She moved to [[Minneapolis–Saint Paul]], Minnesota, to become president of [[Metropolitan State University]], where she worked from 1977 to 1988.<ref name="transcript"/>  She helped to substantially expand the university,<ref name="Grotto"/> and promoted involvement of minorities and women in higher education.<ref name="Equality"/> Her husband joined the Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Company ([[3M]]) as a research chemist.<ref name="transcript"/>

==Business career==
In 1988, King was recruited by General Mills in Minneapolis, Minnesota, to serve in two roles. She became vice president of the [[General Mills Corporation]] and president and executive director of the General Mills Foundation. She remained in these positions from 1988 to 2002. In 2002, she was elected as chairman of the board of trustees of General Mills Foundation, and served in this position for a further year, retiring completely from General Mills in 2003.  Under her leadership the General Mills Foundation, originally established in 1954, has been active both locally and nationally in philanthropic and community service.<ref name="Grotto"/>

King has served  on the boards of a number of other corporations, including [[ExxonMobil]], [[Wells Fargo|Wells Fargo & Company]]; [[Department 56]]; Minnesota Mutual Companies; and the [[H.B. Fuller|H. B. Fuller Company]]. In 1994, she was appointed by President [[Bill Clinton]] to be a member of the Board of Directors of the [[Corporation for National and Community Service]], and served until her resignation in 1997.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://youthtoday.org/2002/07/newsmakers-for-july-2002/|title=Newsmakers for July 2002|work=Youth Today|date=July 1, 2002}}</ref> She has also served with nonprofits, such as the International Trachoma Initiative, [[Allina Health]], the [[Council on Foundations]], the [[National Association of Corporate Directors]],<ref name="Daly">{{cite news|last=Daly|first=Ken|title=NACD Board Names Dr. Reatha Clark King Chairman|url=http://blog.nacdonline.org/2013/05/nacd-board-names-dr-reatha-clark-king-chairman/|access-date=13 May 2014|newspaper=National Association of Corporate Directors|date=23 May 2013}}</ref> and the [[Congressional Black Caucus Foundation]].<ref name="AAR">{{cite news |title=Equality through education and giving, Reatha Clark King |url=https://aaregistry.org/story/equality-through-education-and-giving-reatha-clark-king/ |access-date=24 October 2018 |work=African American Registry}}</ref>

She has served as a trustee with [[Clark Atlanta University]], and is a Life Trustee for the [[University of Chicago]].  She is a member of the [[American Council on Education]] and the Executive Leadership Council in Washington, D.C.<ref name=Bloomberg>{{cite web|title=Reatha Clark King Ph.D. Executive Profile|url=http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/people/person.asp?personId=798105|publisher=Bloomberg BusinessWeek|access-date=16 December 2014}}{{dead link|date=April 2023|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref>
She has a particularly strong interest in education,<ref name="Harvey">{{cite book |last1=King |first1=Reatha Clark |chapter=Succeeding Against the Odds in Higher Education: Advancing Society by Overcoming Obstacles Due to Race and Gender |editor-last=Harvey |editor-first=William B. |title=Grass roots and glass ceilings : African American administrators in predominantly white colleges and universities |date=April 1, 1999 |publisher=State University of New York Press |location=Albany, NY |isbn=978-0791441640 |pages=1–38 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CqKxlo7BNPMC&pg=PA1 |access-date=13 November 2018}}</ref> and has stated:  "I realized early in life that education is our best enabling resource, that technical skills are important, and that my stamina for championing educational opportunity for all people is inexhaustible."<ref name="quote">{{cite web|title=Bios: Reatha Clark King, Woman of Science|url=http://www.bu.edu/lernet/pathways/bios.html|work=Paving the Path Before You|publisher=Pathways|access-date=13 May 2014}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
King has received honorary degrees and many other awards, including:<ref name="transcript"/> 
* The Governor's Civil Rights Legend Award, 2019.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nguyen |first1=Christine |title=Photos: Minnesotans celebrate MLK Day |url=https://www.mprnews.org/story/2019/01/21/photos-minnesotans-celebrate-mlk-day |website=MPR News |date=22 January 2019 |access-date=25 January 2019}}</ref>
* International Citizen Award, 2013, from the International Leadership Institute (ILI), Minneapolis, MN.<ref name=Phil>{{cite news|last1=Bolsta|first1=Phil|title=2013 International Citizen Awards|url=http://tcbmag.com/Leadership/Leaders/2013-International-Citizen-Awards|access-date=16 December 2014|work=Twin Cities Business|date=April 19, 2013}}</ref><ref name="International">{{cite news|title=Reatha Clark King, PhD: International Citizen Award|url=http://tcbmag.com/Leadership/Leaders/2013-International-Citizen-Awards/Reatha-Clark-King,-PhD|access-date=13 May 2014|newspaper=Twin Cities Business|date=19 April 2013}}</ref>
* Louis W. Hill, Jr. Fellow in Philanthropy at the Hubert H. Humphrey Center of the University of Minnesota, 2004.<ref name="Equality"/><ref name="Grotto"/>
* Director of the Year from the National Association of Corporate Directors, 2004.<ref name="Grotto"/>
* One of ''Ebony'' magazine's Top 50 Black Executives in Corporate America, 1992.<ref name="Grotto"/>
* Exceptional Black Scientist Award from CIBA-GEIGY Corporation,<ref name="Grotto"/><ref name=Exceptional>{{cite web|title=Exceptional black scientists collection|url=http://archives.nypl.org/scm/20837|website=New York Public Library Archives & Manuscripts|access-date=16 December 2014}}</ref> 1984.<ref name="transcript"/>
* Defender of Democracy Award from the Washington, D.C. Martin Luther King, Jr. National Memorial Project Foundation.<ref name="Makers"/>
* [[Delta Sigma Theta]] sorority, Minneapolis-St. Paul Alumnae Chapter, 1979.<ref name="transcript"/><ref name="NNDB">{{cite web|title=Reatha Clark King|url=http://www.nndb.com/people/624/000127243/|publisher=NNDB Tracking the entire world|access-date=13 May 2014}}</ref>
